title: Integral rank-one subgroups and Weyl words on a Chevalley lattice
statement:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional rational vector space and $R\subset V\setminus\{0\}$ a reduced crystallographic root system spanning $V$, with coroot functionals $\bar c_\alpha$ and weight lattice $P=\{v\in V:\bar c_\alpha(v)\in\mathbf Z\text{ for every }\alpha\in R\}$ in the conventions of [lem-sfb-root-datum-lattice-embedding]. Let $\mathfrak g,\mathfrak h,h_\delta,e_\alpha,\rho,W,\Omega,\Lambda$ satisfy the Chevalley-basis and faithful-representation conditions of [lem-sfb-chevalley-admissible-representation]: $\mathfrak g$ is split semisimple over $\mathbf Q$, $\rho$ is faithful on finite-dimensional $W$, the nonzero weight spaces $W_\lambda$ have weights $\Omega\subset P$ with $\mathbf Z\Omega=P$, and the full lattice $\Lambda=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\Omega}(\Lambda\cap W_\lambda)$ is stable under every $D_{\alpha,m}=\rho(e_\alpha)^m/m!$, with $\rho(e_\alpha)$ nilpotent. Fix a simple-root base $\Delta$, meaning a subset $\Delta\subseteq R$ which is a basis of $V$ such that every root has integral coordinates in $\Delta$ all nonnegative or all nonpositive. Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], $W_F=\Lambda\otimes_{\mathbf Z}F$, and $T=D_F(P)=\operatorname{Spec}F[P]$, where $F[P]$ has basis $e^\lambda$, multiplication $e^\lambda e^\mu=e^{\lambda+\mu}$, comultiplication $e^\lambda\mapsto e^\lambda\otimes e^\lambda$, counit $e^\lambda\mapsto1$, and antipode $e^\lambda\mapsto e^{-\lambda}$. Embed $T$ in $\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$ by its weight characters on the summands $(\Lambda\cap W_\lambda)\otimes F$. Define the finite polynomial matrices $x_\alpha(a)=\sum_{m\geq0}(D_{\alpha,m}\otimes1)a^m$ for every commutative $F$-algebra. Group schemes and closed subgroups have the meanings of [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup], and $\mathbf G_a,\mathbf G_m$ those of [def-sc-gm-ga]. For every $\alpha\in R$ there is a group-scheme homomorphism $v_\alpha:\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$, where $\operatorname{SL}_2(A)$ consists of determinant-one $2\times2$ matrices, satisfying
$$v_\alpha(I_2+aE_{12})=x_\alpha(a),\quad v_\alpha(I_2+aE_{21})=x_{-\alpha}(a),\quad v_\alpha\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})=h_\alpha(s).$$
Here $I_2$ is the identity matrix, $E_{ij}$ has its single nonzero entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$, and $h_\alpha:\mathbf G_m\to T$ acts on weight $\lambda$ by $s^{\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)}$. Each $x_\alpha$ is a closed immersion of group schemes. The smallest closed subgroup $J_\alpha$ generated by $T,x_\alpha,x_{-\alpha}$ is split reductive, has split maximal torus $T$, roots exactly $\pm\alpha$ and coroot for $\alpha$ equal to $h_\alpha$, in the conventions of [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. For distinct $\alpha,\beta\in\Delta$, the morphisms $x_{-\alpha}$ and $x_\beta$ commute over every $F$-algebra. Put $n_\alpha=x_\alpha(1)x_{-\alpha}(-1)x_\alpha(1)$. Conjugation by $n_\alpha$ normalizes $T$, acts on its characters by $\lambda\mapsto\lambda-\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)\alpha$, and carries $x_\beta(a)$ to $x_{s_\alpha\beta}(\epsilon_{\alpha,\beta}a)$ for fixed signs $\epsilon_{\alpha,\beta}\in\{1,-1\}$. For each $\gamma\in R$ there are $\delta\in\Delta$ and a finite word $n$ in $n_\alpha^{\pm1}$ with $\alpha\in\Delta$ such that $n x_\delta(a)n^{-1}=x_\gamma(\epsilon a)$ for a sign $\epsilon$. All formulas hold as morphism identities, including over nonreduced $F$-algebras and in characteristics two and three. Reductive means smooth connected affine of finite type with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup; unipotent means unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. The assertions indexed by roots are vacuous for $R=\varnothing$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), Theorem 23.72 proof, pp.510-511: rank-one hypotheses and simple-root generation omitted there; Section 23d and Theorem 23.71 for Weyl signs. These integral rank-one details are an agent-stated supporting lemma, not a quotation of Theorem 23.72.

proof.text: Realize the given rational roots and coroots as a finite rational root pairing. The simple roots and coroots are bases of their rational spaces and generate their respective integer root lattices by [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans]; their sign conditions give the base required by [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction]. Apply reflection induction to the dual pairing with the predicate that a coroot is primitive in the integer span of the simple coroots. It holds on a simple coroot because these form an integer basis, is preserved by negation, and is preserved by each simple reflection, an invertible integral map of this lattice. Since $P$ is its integer dual, for every $\alpha$ there is $\lambda_0\in P$ with $\bar c_\alpha(\lambda_0)=1$. Thus $h_\alpha:\mathbf G_m\to T$ is a closed immersion by character antiduality. Also the weight action $T\to\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$ is a closed immersion: in a weight basis its characters are the weights and these generate $P$; the diagonal torus character map is therefore surjective.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: For a fixed root $\alpha$, put $E=\rho(e_\alpha)$, $F_-=\rho(e_{-\alpha})$, $H=\rho(h_\alpha)$. The Chevalley brackets give $[E,F_-]=H$, $[H,E]=2E$ and $[H,F_-]=-2F_-$. Regroup the lattice's weight summands by the integer $j=\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)$. This is an $H$-eigenlattice decomposition. All divided powers of $E,F_-$ are integral and both are nilpotent by the hypotheses. Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-lattice-integration] and base change to $F$. It gives $v_\alpha$ with exactly the displayed upper, lower and diagonal restrictions. In particular the diagonal acts by $s^{\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)}$, so it is the specified $h_\alpha$, with no sign change in the lower parametrization.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: The restriction of $v_\alpha$ to the diagonal torus is the composite of the two closed immersions in step 1. Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-diagonal-kernel-detection] to $v_\alpha$; it is a closed immersion. Its composite with the standard upper unitriangular closed immersion $\mathbf G_a\to\operatorname{SL}_2$ is $x_\alpha$. The upper inclusion is closed directly from the equations $g_{11}=g_{22}=1$, $g_{21}=0$ in the determinant-one coordinate ring. Thus $x_\alpha$ is a closed immersion. This applies to every root, including negative roots.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text:
The bracket $[h,e_\alpha]=\alpha(h)e_\alpha$ implies $D_{\alpha,m}(W_\lambda)\subseteq W_{\lambda+m\alpha}$. Hence, integrally on the weight-decomposed lattice, $t x_\alpha(a)t^{-1}=x_\alpha(\alpha(t)a)$ and $t x_{-\alpha}(a)t^{-1}=x_{-\alpha}(\alpha(t)^{-1}a)$. Consequently
$$t v_\alpha(g)t^{-1}=v_\alpha(C_{\alpha(t)}g),\qquad C_z(g)=\operatorname{diag}(z,1)g\operatorname{diag}(z^{-1},1).$$
Indeed the two sides agree on the diagonal and the two unitriangular subgroups, by the formulas just proved. These determine the morphism on the Gauss chart where the top-left entry is invertible and on its translate by the Weyl matrix; those charts cover $\operatorname{SL}_2$ (the two entries of its first column generate the unit ideal). This proves equivariance as a morphism identity over every test algebra.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text:
Choose $\lambda_0\in P$ with $\bar c_\alpha(\lambda_0)=1$ as in step 1 and let $S=\ker(\lambda_0:T\to\mathbf G_m)$. The decomposition $P=\mathbf Z\lambda_0\oplus\ker\bar c_\alpha$ gives $T=h_\alpha(\mathbf G_m)\times S$, with $S=D_F(\ker\bar c_\alpha)$ a split torus. Define $z(t)=h_\alpha(\alpha(t)^{-1})t^2$ for $t\in S$. Since $\alpha\circ h_\alpha(s)=s^2$, one has $\alpha(z(t))=1$, so step 4 shows that $z(S)$ centralizes $v_\alpha(\operatorname{SL}_2)$. Thus
$$f:\operatorname{SL}_2\times S\longrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(W_F),\quad f(g,t)=v_\alpha(g)z(t)$$
is a homomorphism. On the diagonal torus $D\times S$ its map is $u(s,t)=h_\alpha(s\alpha(t)^{-1})t^2$. Its pullback is injective with finite cokernel: in the displayed product decomposition of $T$ this map is $(s,t)\mapsto(s\alpha(t)^{-1},t^2)$, an automorphism followed by squaring on the second factor.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: Compute the scheme kernel of $f$ over every algebra $A$. If $f(g,t)=1$, then $v_\alpha(g)\in T(A)$, hence commutes after all extensions with $h_\alpha(\mathbf G_m)$. As $v_\alpha$ is a closed immersion, $g$ commutes with $D$. Comparing the two off-diagonal coefficients in $g\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})=\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})g$ over $A[q,q^{-1}]$ shows $g=\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})$. Therefore $\ker f=\ker u$ as subgroup schemes of $D\times S$. Writing $N=u^*P\subset X^*(D\times S)$, it follows that $\ker f=D_F(X^*(D\times S)/N)$. Moreover $u^*\alpha(s,t)=s^2$. Thus $N$ contains the two roots $\pm(2,0)$ of $\operatorname{SL}_2\times S$, and on $\ker u$ one has $s^2=1$; its first matrix component is scalar and the kernel is central. No passage from geometric points to schemes has been used.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: The group $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is semisimple by [lem-sfb-sl2-universal-multiplicative-cover]. Its diagonal is a split maximal torus (a commuting $2\times2$ matrix is diagonal), its roots are $\pm2$ by conjugating the off-diagonal tangent matrices, and its coroot is $s\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(s,s^{-1})$: the Weyl matrix inverts this torus, giving the reflection formula $m\mapsto-m=m-m\cdot2$. Apply [lem-sfb-central-character-sublattice-quotient] with $H=\operatorname{SL}_2$, $C=X^*(S)$ and the finite-index sublattice $N$ of step 6. It gives a split reductive quotient $Q=(\operatorname{SL}_2\times S)/\ker f$ whose split maximal torus is $(D\times S)/\ker u$, with roots pulling back to $\pm(2,0)$ and with the coroot induced by the standard diagonal of $\operatorname{SL}_2$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: Factor $f$ as a faithfully flat homomorphism onto a closed subgroup $I\subset\operatorname{GL}(W_F)$ using [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image]. Its kernel is the same $\ker f$ as the quotient map to $Q$. Apply [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal] to each map to obtain inverse homomorphisms $I\leftrightarrow Q$; their composites become the identity after the respective faithfully flat maps from $\operatorname{SL}_2\times S$, hence are the identity. The image torus is $T$ since $u$ has character image $N$ and quotient $(D\times S)/\ker u\simeq T$. The closed subgroup $I$ contains $T$ and $v_\alpha(\operatorname{SL}_2)$, hence $x_{\pm\alpha}$. Conversely these three subgroups generate a subgroup containing the image of $f$, since $z(t)\in T$ and $\operatorname{SL}_2$ is generated by its two unitriangular subgroups and diagonal on its two Gauss charts. Therefore $I=J_\alpha$. Transporting the root data of step 7 along $u$ gives roots exactly $\pm\alpha$, and its coroot maps $s$ to $u(s,1)=h_\alpha(s)$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: For distinct simple roots $\alpha,\beta$, $\beta-\alpha$ is neither a root nor zero: its simple coordinates have both signs. The Chevalley bracket therefore gives $[e_{-\alpha},e_\beta]=0$. Their representation operators commute, and hence so do their finite exponentials over $\mathbf Q[a,b]$. Each matrix entry of both products belongs to $\mathbf Z[a,b]$ by lattice admissibility. The injection $\mathbf Z[a,b]\to\mathbf Q[a,b]$ makes the equality integral. Base change proves $x_{-\alpha}(a)x_\beta(b)=x_\beta(b)x_{-\alpha}(a)$ over every $F$-algebra.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-adjoint-weyl-signs]. Over $\mathbf Q$, conjugation of a represented Lie element by $\exp(\rho e)$ equals its image under $\exp(\operatorname{ad}e)$: expanding the two exponentials gives the coefficient $\sum_{i+j=m}(-1)^j E^iYE^j/(i!j!)=(\operatorname{ad}E)^m(Y)/m!$. Thus $n_\alpha\rho(e_\beta)n_\alpha^{-1}=\epsilon_{\alpha,\beta}\rho(e_{s_\alpha\beta})$. Taking the finite exponential in parameter $a$ yields $n_\alpha x_\beta(a)n_\alpha^{-1}=x_{s_\alpha\beta}(\epsilon_{\alpha,\beta}a)$. Both sides have integral polynomial matrices; $n_\alpha^{-1}$ is integral because $x_\gamma(a)^{-1}=x_\gamma(-a)$. Therefore the identity descends from $\mathbf Q[a]$ to $\mathbf Z[a]$ and then to every $F$-algebra, with the same fixed signs.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: The same adjoint identity gives $n_\alpha\rho(h)n_\alpha^{-1}=\rho(h-\alpha(h)h_\alpha)$ over $\mathbf Q$. It follows directly from the eigenvalue equations that $n_\alpha W_\lambda=W_{s_\alpha\lambda}$: substituting $h-\alpha(h)h_\alpha$ into $\lambda$ gives $\lambda-\bar c_\alpha(\lambda)\alpha$. The integral inverse shows $n_\alpha(\Lambda\cap W_\lambda)=\Lambda\cap W_{s_\alpha\lambda}$. Thus after every base change $n_\alpha$ permutes the weight summands by this reflection, and conjugates their scalar character action by the induced automorphism of $P$. This proves scheme-theoretic normalization of $T$ and precisely the stated character reflection, even when two differentiated weights coincide in positive characteristic.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153) and omitted rank-one verification in Theorem 23.72, pp.510--511; agent expansion.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction] to the predicate $Q(\gamma)$: there are $\delta\in\Delta$ and simple roots $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$ ($k\geq0$) such that $\gamma=w\delta$ for $w=s_{\alpha_1}\cdots s_{\alpha_k}$ and, for $n=n_{\alpha_1}\cdots n_{\alpha_k}$ and some sign $\epsilon$, $n x_\delta(a)n^{-1}=x_\gamma(\epsilon a)$. Iterating step 10 along the word gives, for every root $\beta$, $n x_\beta(a)n^{-1}=x_{w\beta}(\epsilon' a)$ with a sign $\epsilon'$ depending on $\beta$ and the word. A simple root has the empty word. Simple reflection: if $Q(\gamma)$ holds via $(\delta,w,n)$ and $\alpha\in\Delta$, the word $n_\alpha n$ and $s_\alpha w$ give $Q(s_\alpha\gamma)$ by step 10, with the product of the signs. Negation: if $Q(\gamma)$ holds via $(\delta,w,n)$, use the word $n n_\delta$ and $ws_\delta$. Then $ws_\delta\delta=-w\delta=-\gamma$, and $n n_\delta x_\delta(a)n_\delta^{-1}n^{-1}=n x_{-\delta}(\epsilon_{\delta,\delta}a)n^{-1}=x_{-\gamma}(\epsilon_{\delta,\delta}\epsilon' a)$ by step 10 and the iterated identity for $\beta=-\delta$. This verifies the three hypotheses of the induction leaf and proves the word assertion for all roots; only the $n_\alpha$ with $\alpha\in\Delta$ occur. Every earlier identity was integral or an identity of group-scheme morphisms, so it remains valid on nonreduced algebras and in characteristics two and three. If $R=\varnothing$, there is no root-indexed assertion to prove.
